# Vedanā Saṁyutta (SN 36)

**ID:** SN 36
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Vedanā Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0304m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vedanā Saṁyutta* (SN 36) is the thirty-sixth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, located in the *Saḷāyatanavagga* ("The Book of the Six Sense Bases") [Bodhi 2003]. While the Burmese tradition and the Pali Text Society edition present it as an independent *saṁyutta*, the Sinhalese manuscript tradition incorporates it as a subchapter of the preceding *Saḷāyatanasaṁyutta* (SN 35) [Bodhi 2003]. The collection comprises 31 discourses centered on the three types of feeling (*vedanā*): pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Here, *vedanā* signifies the hedonic or affective tone of experience rather than emotional complexity; because feeling arises from sensory contact and directly stimulates craving in dependent origination, understanding and detaching from it links doctrinal analysis with the practical cultivation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) [Bodhi 2003].

Prominent discourses in the collection explore sickness, meditation, and psychological suffering. The well-known *Sallasutta* (SN 36.6) uses the simile of two darts to contrast the worldling with the noble disciple: while both experience bodily pain (the first dart), the mindful practitioner avoids generating mental anguish (the second dart) [Wen; Anālayo 2016]. In the *Gelaññasuttas* (SN 36.7 and SN 36.8), the Buddha visits ill monastics, encouraging mindfulness and comparing the eventual cooling of feelings at death to an oil lamp expiring when its fuel is spent [Wen; Anālayo 2016]. Other suttas present evocative imagery, such as diverse winds (SN 36.12) or guests arriving at a guest house (SN 36.14), to convey the transient nature of varied feelings [Anālayo 2014]. Sutta 11 (*Rahogatasutta*) delineates the sequential calming (*passaddhi*) and cessation of functions, noting that respiration ceases in the fourth *jhāna* [Kuan]. Verses throughout the collection summarize insight into feelings within the framework of the Four Noble Truths [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2014]. In addition to Bhikkhu Bodhi's complete translation, the samyutta was translated into English with an introduction by Ñāṇaponika Thera [Bodhi 2003; Anālayo 2014].

 DharmaNexus indicates widespread Pali-internal reuse, recording over 12,000 matching passages across 341 texts, with its largest textual overlaps occurring with the *Bahuvedanīya Sutta* (MN 59 §19.1.1_0–19.6.3 ↔ §1.3_0–6.3), the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), and the *Saḷāyatanasaṁyutta* (SN 35) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language matches in DharmaNexus further corroborate alignment with the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) as well as citations preserved in Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, *Śrāvakabhūmi*, and *Abhidharmāmṛta* [DharmaNexus].
